vignette:
He was sixty-four when the accident happened, but he still remembers every second of it as if it were happening right now. It was a Tuesday afternoon in late autumn, the sky a pale, washed-out blue. He had been driving home from the cemetery, where he had placed a small pine wreath on his wife’s grave. She had been gone three years by then, and the visits had become a routine he kept, a quiet hour of nothing but her name on the headstone. That day, the road was slick with wet leaves. He stopped at a green light, waited for it to turn, then eased into the intersection. He never saw the pickup coming from the left. The driver had run a red light at nearly sixty miles per hour.

The impact spun his sedan into a light pole. He remembers the sound—a deep, metallic groan that seemed to come from inside his own chest. The airbag hit him in the face, and for a moment there was only white pressure and the smell of burned powder. Then he opened his eyes and saw blood on his hands. Not his own—the passenger seat had crumpled inward, and he realized with a cold, distant clarity that his side had taken the brunt because he had instinctively leaned into the wheel, trying to brace for a blast. That was when the old training kicked in. He had been a medic in the army for twenty-two years, then another fifteen as a paramedic. He knew how to triage a scene, how to stay calm when others are screaming. He unbuckled his belt, climbed out of the wreck, and started checking the other driver. The pickup’s cab was intact; the driver was dazed but conscious. He told him to stay still, called 911, and waited. He did everything right.

But something in him broke that day, and he knew it even before the paramedics arrived—the real paramedics, the ones who came for him. He felt it as a strange hollow in his chest, a quiet, humming emptiness that would not fill back up.

Now he is sixty-seven, and that hollow has only grown wider. He cannot drive. He sold the sedan two months after the accident and now takes the bus or asks his daughter for rides. He lives alone in the same house he shared with his wife, but he has moved the furniture out of the living room because the shape of the sofa reminds him of the way the door folded inward. He sleeps in the guest room now, with the curtains drawn and a small lamp on. The nightmares come almost every night—not the collision itself, but the moment after, when he is standing on the side of the road and realizes he does not know where his wife is, and he starts searching for her among the broken glass. He wakes up with his hands shaking, reaching for a medical bag that is no longer there.

He spent thirty-seven years responding to emergencies. Now he flinches at the sound of a car horn. He avoids intersections on his walks, taking long detours through parks and alleys. He does not talk about the accident, not even to his daughter. When she asks, he says he is fine, and she knows not to push. He stopped going to the cemetery, too. Not because he does not miss his wife—he misses her with a sharp, physical ache—but because the drive takes him past that intersection. He has not been able to bring himself to look at it. At night, he sits in the darkened kitchen and thinks about the pickup driver, who walked away with a broken arm and a concussion. He wonders if that man still drives. He wonders if he ever thinks about the old man in the sedan who crawled out of the wreck and told him to stay still. He wonders if anyone remembers that he used to know exactly what to do.
